blocks.text: Give each screen a view model that exposes observable state and commands, and let a thin view bind to it.

The **view model** holds presentation state (field values, enabled flags, messages) and the actions the user can trigger. It imports no UI classes. The **view** only binds: widgets observe properties, and user events call commands. The UI logic therefore becomes plain objects that tests drive directly.
Binding needs an observable type. Most platforms provide one: JavaFX properties, Android `LiveData` or `StateFlow`, SwiftUI `@Published`.

walkthrough.note: A minimal observable value. `bind` delivers the current value immediately and every later change, and `set` ignores no-op writes.
The view model derives `canSubmit` from two inputs and exposes a command. It depends on a model-side `BiPredicate`, never on a widget.
The view's whole job: subscribe widgets to properties. Println stands in for button and label updates.
User events are just `set` calls on properties. Only the password that crosses 8 characters flips `canSubmit`, so no redundant events appear.

blocks.text: A mobile checkout screen with asynchronous price updates.

The checkout view model exposes `lines`, `total`, `isLoading`, `error` and a `placeOrder` command. The price service updates `total`; the screen redraws because it observes state. Rotating the device recreates the view while the view model survives, and tests assert on `canPlaceOrder` without launching an emulator.

lines: // the screen: observe state, call placeOrder()

blocks.text: Payoff: screen logic is unit-tested as plain objects, and the view survives configuration changes without losing state.

lists.title: Use when
items: The UI framework supports data binding or reactive state.
Screen logic is substantial and deserves fast unit tests.
State must outlive the view, as on rotation.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The platform lacks binding and you'd hand-write synchronization everywhere.
The screen is static; a view model is ceremony.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: The view model holding a reference to the view or context, leaking it.
Binding logic hidden in markup, where tests can't reach it.
Exposing mutable state so the view can corrupt it.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A view model per widget instead of per screen.
Fields mirrored in model, view model and DTO with no transformation.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: JavaFX properties and `javafx.beans.binding.Bindings` are the JDK-adjacent binding tools.
Records suit immutable state snapshots exposed by a view model.

rows.difference: In MVC the view observes the domain model and a controller handles input. In MVVM the view binds, often two-way, to a view model holding view-specific state and commands, and needs no controller.
Binding is Observer: the view subscribes to view-model properties. MVVM adds the role split around that mechanism.
View-model actions are often exposed as command objects that the view can invoke and enable or disable.
The view model adapts domain data to what a screen needs, but it also owns presentation state and behavior, which an adapter doesn't.

options.why: Observable state plus a command, with a screen that merely subscribes and forwards events.
The screen subscribes to state derived for it (`enabled`), not to a domain model, and no separate controller handles input.
Observer is the mechanism, but the class also owns presentation state and an action for the view.
The enabled flag is data, not a swappable object that changes the class's behavior.

options.why: A UI-free view model holds the state and survives view recreation, and the view just binds.
A controller that pokes widgets ties logic to the view and makes rotation handling manual.
Observer is just the notification part; it doesn't say where screen state and commands live.
A facade would simplify the backend call, not organize presentation state.

exercises.prompt: Explain MVVM: what the view model contains, what the view does, and why it helps testing.

modelAnswer.text: The view model holds presentation state as observable properties and exposes commands for user actions, with no reference to any widget. The view only binds widgets to those properties and forwards events. Because the view model is plain code, tests set inputs and assert on outputs without a UI.

keyPoints: View model: observable state plus commands
No UI classes in the view model
View only binds and forwards events
Tests drive the view model directly
Differs from MVC: the view binds to presentation state, not the domain model
